title: AlexNet – The Model That Sparked the Deep Learning Boom
description: A look into AlexNet, the breakthrough CNN that won ImageNet 2012 and changed the trajectory of deep learning.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation If LeNet was the blueprint, AlexNet was the explosion. In 2012, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton entered the ImageNet competition with a deep CNN. The result shocked everyone: their model crushed the competition with a top-5 error of 15.3% compared to the next best at 26.2%. That’s not just a win, that’s a landslide. This single result is what most people point to as the moment that started the modern deep learning boom. For me, it was also the first "big" CNN I read about after LeNet. It showed me that the same ideas could scale up if you had enough data and enough compute. Back then, GPUs weren’t commonly used for neural networks. AlexNet was the first to really lean on GPUs for training, and that’s what made it possible to train a network this large. ## Model Breakdown AlexNet is much bigger than LeNet, but it’s not complicated once you see the pattern. Here’s a layer-by-layer look: - **Input:** 224×224 RGB image from ImageNet (1000 classes). - **Conv1:** 96 filters of size 11×11, stride 4 → 55×55 feature maps. - **Max Pooling:** 3×3, stride 2. - **Conv2:** 256 filters of size 5×5. - **Max Pooling:** 3×3, stride 2. - **Conv3:** 384 filters of size 3×3. - **Conv4:** 384 filters of size 3×3. - **Conv5:** 256 filters of size 3×3. - **Max Pooling:** 3×3, stride 2. - **FC1:** 4096 units. - **FC2:** 4096 units. - **Output:** 1000 units with softmax. So compared to LeNet, AlexNet just stacks more convolution layers and makes them wider. One thing you might notice in some AlexNet diagrams is that the architecture looks split into two parallel streams. That wasn’t a design choice for accuracy — it was because the model was too large for a single GPU in 2012, so the authors divided it across two GPUs and linked them at certain layers. ## Why the Design Choices Matter **ReLU activations** Instead of tanh, AlexNet used ReLU. This made training much faster because ReLU doesn’t saturate in the positive domain. Today ReLU (or its variants) is the default. **Dropout** The fully connected layers had dropout, which randomly turns off some neurons during training. This was a clever way to reduce overfitting. **Data augmentation** They trained with random crops and flips of images. That might sound basic, but it was a big deal at the time because it helped the model generalize better. **GPUs** AlexNet was split across two GPUs because a single one couldn’t handle the full model. This parallelization was another first for deep learning. ## Implementation Notes Here’s a PyTorch version of AlexNet that matches the original design: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class AlexNet(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes=1000): super(AlexNet, self).__init__() self.features = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 96, kernel_size=11, stride=4, padding=2), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2), nn.Conv2d(96, 256, kernel_size=5, padding=2), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2), nn.Conv2d(256, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(384, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(384, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2), ) self.classifier = nn.Sequential( nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(256 * 6 * 6, 4096), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Dropout(), nn.Linear(4096, 4096), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Linear(4096, num_classes), ) def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = x.view(x.size(0), 256 * 6 * 6) x = self.classifier(x) return x ``` When I trained this on a subset of ImageNet, the model quickly became computationally heavy compared to LeNet or even smaller CNNs. It made me appreciate just how critical GPUs were for the success of AlexNet. Without them, the training time would have been completely unrealistic. ## Reflections Reading about AlexNet made me realize how much of progress in deep learning comes down to scaling. The ideas weren’t brand new. Convolutions, pooling, and fully connected layers were already there in LeNet. What AlexNet added was size, data, GPUs, and a few clever tricks like ReLU and dropout. After AlexNet, things snowballed. VGG showed that depth with small filters could work even better. GoogLeNet focused on efficiency with inception modules. ResNet solved the vanishing gradient problem with skip connections. But if you trace back all of those, AlexNet was the model that kicked the door open.
